textbook:
Clean cutaway textbook illustration of a SINGLE Clostridioides difficile bacterium, centered in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame with generous negative space around it for later labels. Semi-flat vector-style shading, crisp clean boundaries between structures, a MUTED desaturated educational palette of soft dusty tints, THIN clean outlines and gentle soft shading, on a neutral dark charcoal background. Never bright primary or cartoon colours, never heavy black cartoon strokes.

SHAPE — this is the whole point of the figure. The cell is a LONG, SLENDER, GENTLY CURVED ROD lying on a shallow diagonal from lower left to upper right, about SEVEN TIMES LONGER THAN IT IS WIDE, with smoothly rounded poles. Near ONE END of the rod — roughly one fifth to one quarter of the way in from that pole, clearly NOT at the very tip and emphatically NOT in the middle of the cell — sits a large oval ENDOSPORE that SWELLS AND BULGES THE ROD OUTWARD at that spot, so the silhouette reads as a CLUB or TENNIS RACQUET: a smooth slim shaft that fattens into a rounded knob near one end and then narrows again to the short stub of cell beyond it. That asymmetric bulge is the single most important feature of the picture.

SPORE POSITION IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT DETAIL IN THIS PICTURE AND ALSO THE MOST COMMON ERROR. The endospore is SUBTERMINAL: not terminal, not at the tip, not at mid-cell. Put the CENTRE of the spore about ONE THIRD of the way along the rod measured from the nearer pole. A CLEAR, UNMISTAKABLE LENGTH OF ORDINARY SLIM ROD — at least as long as the spore itself, keeping the shaft's normal slim width and ending in its own smoothly rounded pole — MUST CONTINUE BEYOND THE SWELLING to that end of the cell. The spore must NOT be the last thing along the silhouette, must NOT form the cap or tip of the cell, and must NOT touch the pole. Picture a slim snake that has swallowed an egg a little way behind its head. The swelling is a MODERATE oval bulge, roughly one and a half to twice the shaft's width — never a huge balloon several times wider than the rod, and never so large that the cell reads as a lollipop or a tadpole.

ENVELOPE — this bacterium is GRAM-POSITIVE, so from the outside in there are exactly three envelope layers and NO outer membrane: (1) an outermost thin, finely stippled, pale slate-blue paracrystalline S-LAYER shown as a delicate regular tiled skin; (2) beneath it a CONSPICUOUSLY THICK sage-green PEPTIDOGLYCAN CELL WALL drawn as a broad homogeneous band, clearly the thickest layer of the envelope; (3) beneath that a thin muted violet PLASMA MEMBRANE. There must be NO second outer membrane, NO periplasmic gap between two membranes, and NO shaggy LPS or O-antigen fringe.

CUTAWAY: a quarter of the envelope is peeled back along the upper side of the rod in a long soft-edged window that follows the cell's gentle curve, so the three envelope layers are visible in section as three distinct stacked bands and the interior is on show. Inside: a pale warm ivory-sand CYTOPLASM holding an irregular, loosely folded, cloud-like dusty blue-purple NUCLEOID (a diffuse tangle of DNA fibrils, never a tidy little circle or ring) and numerous tiny scattered teal RIBOSOME dots. The ENDOSPORE is also shown in section as concentric layers: a dense pale-gold spore CORE at the centre, around it a broad pale sage CORTEX, around that a layered dark umber-brown SPORE COAT of several fine ridged laminations, and outermost a thin, loose, slightly wrinkled grey-brown EXOSPORIUM balloon standing a little away from the coat. The spore sits fully INSIDE the mother cell, enclosed by the mother cell's own envelope — never floating free outside the rod.

FLAGELLA: about seven to nine long, slender, gently wavy coral-pink FLAGELLA emerge PERITRICHOUSLY — that is, from many points scattered all over the sides and both ends of the rod, not from one tuft and not only from the poles — and trail loosely outward into the empty background.

Do NOT draw a Gram-negative double envelope, an outer membrane, LPS or an O-antigen fringe; no thick polysaccharide capsule or halo; no coccus, sphere or grape-cluster; no spore in the middle of the cell and no spore free-floating outside it; no geometric or icosahedral virus capsid; no mesosome; no tidy circular DNA loop; no membrane-bound organelles (no nucleus, mitochondria, ER or Golgi); no second cell or chain of cells; no gut wall, food or scene props. Anatomically faithful, single specimen only. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, labels, scale bars, arrows or watermarks, and fill the whole square edge-to-edge with no border, frame, vignette or letterbox.

THE BACKGROUND IS COMPLETELY EMPTY. No extra floating object of any kind: no shell, fan, tassel, brush, tuft, frill, feather, torn paper shred, crystal, bubble, debris speck or second organism anywhere in the frame, and nothing attached to either pole of the cell except the flagella themselves.

FINALLY: the two poles of the cell are BARE, SMOOTH and ROUNDED. Do not attach, draw or suggest any frill, ruffle, paper cap, tassel, feathered plume, shredded fan, splash, brush end, shell or crown at either end of the cell or anywhere else. This is a bacterium, not a chicken drumstick, not a paintbrush and not a flower.

PROPORTIONS, FINAL AND NON-NEGOTIABLE: the cell must be LONG AND SLENDER — at least SEVEN TIMES LONGER THAN IT IS WIDE. A long thin sausage or a length of slim tubing, NOT a fat bean, NOT a short stubby capsule, NOT an egg. And the spore's swelling must be OBVIOUS: at the spore the outline visibly BULGES OUTWARD to about one and a half times the shaft's width and then NARROWS BACK DOWN to the normal slim shaft ON BOTH SIDES of the spore — there is slim rod before it and slim rod after it. THE SPORE MUST NOT CAP, CLOSE OR FORM THE END OF THE CELL: beyond the swelling, a clearly visible length of ordinary slim rod continues on and ends in its own smooth rounded pole.

GEOMETRY OF THE SPORE — FOLLOW THIS LITERALLY, IT OVERRIDES EVERYTHING ELSE. Divide the rod's long axis into TEN equal segments numbered 1 to 10 from one pole to the other. The endospore occupies ONLY segments 3, 4 and 5. Segments 1 and 2 must be drawn in full as ORDINARY SLIM UN-SWOLLEN ROD — a plain slim length of bacterium with its own envelope, its own cytoplasm, its own scattered ribosome dots and its own smooth rounded pole. Segments 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 are likewise ordinary slim rod ending in a smooth rounded pole. The spore therefore has PLAIN SLIM ROD ON BOTH SIDES OF IT and reaches NEITHER pole. If the spore touches a pole, caps the end, or is the last thing you meet travelling along the cell, THE PICTURE IS WRONG.
